passage: Every evening after homework, Kunal stood at his window in the Kolkata flat and tossed a rolled-up sock into his open laundry basket. He kept missing. Last night he told his friend Samir on the phone, “I'm going to practise basketball every day for a month.” Samir said, “Every day? Isn't that a lot?” Kunal thought and changed it. “Okay, I'll shoot ten times after homework, every day this week.” The next evening he counted ten throws. He made three, and grinned. He pinned a small card on his wall, wrote “Ten throws,” and ticked the first box.

qa.q: How many throws did Kunal plan each evening?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel about his plan after Samir asked if it was a lot?
qa.a: He thought again and decided his big declaration was too much, so he chose a smaller plan he could actually keep.

qa.q: Why is Kunal's second plan more likely to work?
qa.a: It is small and specific, ten throws after homework for one week, and he made a card to tick it off.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Kunal changed the plan?
qa.a: He probably felt glad that his question helped, and maybe a bit proud of his friend.

grounding: A child declares an intention and revises it into a small, specific plan, which is more likely to succeed.

passage: “I am going to learn the whole tabla in one week,” Nikita announced at the dinner table. Her father raised an eyebrow. “The whole thing?” “Yes! Every day, for hours!” Gautam, her cousin, laughed. “You said that about the drawing, too.” Nikita frowned. “That time I forgot.” After a pause she said, “Okay, maybe I'll practise ten minutes after dinner, and learn the first beat by Sunday.” Her father nodded. “That sounds like something you can do.” Nikita wrote “ten minutes, first beat” on her hand with a pen, and grinned at Gautam.

qa.q: How many minutes did Nikita decide to practise?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What made Nikita change her declaration?
qa.a: Her cousin's remark about the drawing, and her father's raised eyebrow, made her realise the first plan was too big, so she chose a smaller step.

qa.q: Why did her father say the new plan sounds doable?
qa.a: It is small and specific, ten minutes after dinner and the first beat by Sunday.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt about reminding Nikita of the drawing?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit teasing but also caring, since her new plan showed she listened. 🙂

grounding: A child declares I am going to learn everything and then reshapes it into a small, specific plan.

passage: I'm Tushar. Last summer I announced at dinner, “I'm going to practise cricket every single day and be the best bowler in the colony.” Everyone clapped. I practised on Monday. On Tuesday it rained. By Friday I'd forgotten. My uncle Kishore didn't tease me. He said, “Big plan, no steps. Try this: twenty balls at one stump, after school, Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Mark them on the calendar.” It sounded too small. But I did it. After a month I could hit the stump eight times out of twenty. I didn't become the best bowler in the colony. I did become better than I was.

qa.q: How many balls did Kishore suggest Tushar bowl each time?
qa.a: He suggested twenty balls at one stump.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when the family clapped at dinner?
qa.a: Tushar felt proud and excited about the big plan.

qa.q: Why did Kishore's plan work better than the first declaration?
qa.a: It was small and specific, with a set number, set days and a calendar, so Tushar could actually keep it up.

qa.q: How did Kishore react when the first plan fell apart?
qa.a: Kishore didn't tease; he calmly pointed out the plan had no steps and offered a smaller one.

grounding: Shows a child's big, vague declaration fading and a small, specific plan succeeding.

passage: Library note, Monday. Jomon, Class 4 teacher. Zeenat announced to the class today, “This year I'm going to read a hundred books!” The class was impressed. I've heard this from other children, and usually it fades by the second week. So at break I asked her, “What's the first step?” She looked puzzled. “Read… a lot?” We made it smaller together: two chapters every night before brushing her teeth, ticked on a chart stuck to her cupboard. She chose the first book herself. I'll check the chart with her every Monday. A hundred books is a wonderful dream. Two chapters tonight is a plan.

qa.q: Where is Zeenat's chart stuck?
qa.a: The chart is stuck to her cupboard.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when asked about the first step?
qa.a: Zeenat felt puzzled, since she hadn't thought beyond the big, exciting goal.

qa.q: What small, specific plan did Jomon help Zeenat make?
qa.a: Two chapters every night before brushing her teeth, ticked on a chart, with a check every Monday.

qa.q: How did the class react to Zeenat's announcement?
qa.a: The class was impressed by the idea of reading a hundred books.

grounding: Shows a child declaring a big goal and a teacher helping turn it into a small, specific plan.

passage: Sunday. Elizabeth's diary. I've decided: I'm going to be amazing at the keyboard by Christmas. I told Arohi on the phone, and she said, “That's what you said about skating.” Rude. But true. I quit skating after three days. So this time I'm writing it smaller, here, so I have to see it. Plan: ten minutes every day after tea. Monday to Friday, scales. Saturday, one new song. Sunday, off. A sticker on the calendar for every day I do it. Arohi said she'll ask me every Friday how many stickers I have. Today was Sunday, so no practice. Tomorrow: ten minutes. That's all.

qa.q: When will Elizabeth practise each day?
qa.a: Elizabeth will practise for ten minutes every day after tea.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Arohi mentioned skating?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt a little stung and annoyed at first, but admitted Arohi was right.

qa.q: Why is Elizabeth's new plan more likely to work?
qa.a: It is small and specific, with set times, tasks for each day, stickers and a Friday check-in with Arohi.

qa.q: How is Arohi helping Elizabeth keep the plan?
qa.a: Arohi will ask every Friday how many stickers Elizabeth has, keeping the plan honest.

grounding: Shows a child moving from a big, vague declaration to a small, specific practice plan.

passage:
After the temple fair, where a boy from the next village had played the harmonium so fast the crowd clapped along, Tanvir burst into the courtyard. "I'm going to practise every single day and be the best harmonium player in the whole district!"

His cousin Mahima, shelling peas, looked up. "Last month you were going to be the best kabaddi raider."

Tanvir scowled. "This is different."
"Okay. Then make it small. What will you practise tomorrow, and when?"
Tanvir thought. "The first line of the aarti tune. After milking, before school. Ten minutes."
"Write it on the wall calendar."

He did, in big crooked letters. Five mornings later, the first line of the aarti was floating across the courtyard, a little wobbly.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir write his plan?
qa.a: On the wall calendar, in big crooked letters.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he burst into the courtyard?
qa.a: Excited and inspired after watching the harmonium player at the fair, eager to be the best 😊

qa.q: What turned Tanvir's big declaration into something that worked?
qa.a: Mahima helped him make it small and specific: the first line of the aarti tune, ten minutes after milking, written on the calendar.

qa.q: How did Mahima see Tanvir's big declaration?
qa.a: Mahima was doubtful, remembering last month's kabaddi plan, but still helped make it workable.

grounding: It shows a child declaring a big goal and a cousin helping turn it into a small, specific plan that succeeds.
